prompt: We have a Leaflet app with a few tile layers and some L.geoJSON overlays, and we now want to serve our own vector tiles and style them in the browser. ## TL;DR 1. **Drop Leaflet** – create a plain MapLibre GL JS map. 2. **Pick a vector-tile basemap** (hosted service, self-hosted TileJSON/PMTiles, or your own tiles). 3. **Write a style JSON** that references that basemap as a `vector` source and adds any of your existing data as separate sources (`geojson` for small overlays, `vector` for large ones). 4. **Port the Leaflet overlay code** to MapLibre source-/layer-calls (the mapping is 1-to-1 for most operations). 5. **Use the migration docs** – the “Leaflet migration guide” and the “maplibre-source-wiring” skill give you the exact “Leaflet → MapLibre” mapping table. Below is a step-by-step walk-through, the exact code equivalents, and the places you should read next. --- ## 1. Why you can (and should) ditch Leaflet | Leaflet feature | MapLibre GL JS equivalent | Why it’s fine to drop Leaflet | |-----------------|--------------------------|------------------------------| | `L.map(container, options)` | `new maplibregl.Map({container, style, center, zoom, ...})` | MapLibre creates the canvas and the WebGL context itself. | | `L.tileLayer(urlTemplate)` | `type: 'vector'` or `type: 'raster'` source in a style JSON | Tile layers are now *sources*; the style decides how they are drawn. | | `L.geoJSON(data, options)` | `type: 'geojson'` source + one or more layers | Same data, but you control paint/layout via the style spec. | | `layer.on('click', …)` | `map.on('click', 'layer-id', …)` | MapLibre’s event system works on *layer IDs* rather than Leaflet layer objects. | | UI controls (zoom, attribution) | `map.addControl(new maplibregl.NavigationControl())` etc. | All built-in controls are provided by MapLibre; you can still use third-party UI libs if you like. | > **Bottom line:** MapLibre already does everything Leaflet was giving you (canvas, controls, interaction). Keeping Leaflet just to “host a second map” adds an extra DOM element, extra event handling, and a second rendering pipeline – unnecessary overhead. --- ## 2. Choose a vector-tile basemap source | Option | How to reference it in a style | When to use it | |--------|-------------------------------|----------------| | **Hosted public style** (e.g. MapTiler, OpenFreeMap, OSM-France) | `style: 'https://.../style.json'` (no extra source needed) | Quick prototype, no tile-server ops. | | **Self-hosted TileJSON** | Add a `vector` source:
`{type:'vector', url:'https://myhost/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf'}` | You already have a TileJSON endpoint or want full control. | | **PMTiles (single-file archive)** | `type:'vector'`, `url:'pmtiles://mytiles.pmtiles'` (requires the PMTiles plugin) | Offline kiosk, demo, or when you want a single file on a CDN. | | **Raster imagery** (satellite, WMS) | `type:'raster'` source + `tiles` array | When you need imagery underneath vector labels. | > **Tip:** If you only need a basemap and you have no custom tiles yet, start with a hosted style URL. You can later replace it with your own vector source without touching the rest of the code. --- ## 3. Build a minimal style JSON A style is just a JSON object. Below is a **bare-bones** example that: * pulls a vector basemap from a TileJSON URL, * adds a small GeoJSON overlay (your former `L.geoJSON`), * inserts the overlay **before the first symbol layer** so your polygons don’t get hidden by road labels. ```json { "version": 8, "sources": { "basemap": { "type": "vector", "url": "https://mytileserver.com/tileset.json" }, "myOverlay": { "type": "geojson", "data": "/data/overlay.geojson" } }, "layers": [ /* 1️⃣ Insert basemap layers – copy from the source style or keep empty and let the source provide them */ { "id": "basemap-background", "type": "background", "paint": { "background-color": "#e0e0e0" } }, { "id": "basemap-land", "type": "fill", "source": "basemap", "source-layer": "land", "paint": { "fill-color": "#f5f5f5" } }, /* 2️⃣ Insert your overlay *before* the first symbol layer (labels) */ { "id": "my-polygon-fill", "type": "fill", "source": "myOverlay", "paint": { "fill-color": "#0080ff", "fill-opacity": 0.4 } }, /* 3️⃣ Let the basemap’s label layers render on top */ { "id": "basemap-labels", "type": "symbol", "source": "basemap", "source-layer": "place_label", "layout": { "text-field": "{name_en}", "text-size": 12 }, "paint": { "text-color": "#222" } } ], "glyphs": "https://myhost/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", "sprite": "https://myhost/sprite" } ``` *If you already have a full style JSON from a provider, you can simply add the `"myOverlay"` source and a few layers to it – no need to rewrite the whole thing.* --- ## 4.
